question: A page omits `<meta charset>` but includes `<title>Café</title>`. How do browsers determine encoding before parsing the title?
options: content-type header signals encoding to the parser before the meta tag is read
charset meta is not needed if the server sends the correct content-type
browsers guess encoding from the first non-ascii character
the title is parsed as bytes until charset is discovered
explanation: The HTTP Content-Type header (e.g., `text/html; charset=utf-8`) is read before the HTML parser starts, so the parser uses server-declared encoding from the beginning.

question: A document has `<html lang='en-US'>` but client JavaScript sets `document.documentElement.lang = 'es'`. Which language do screen readers announce?
options: en-US because the html attribute is the source of truth
es because javascript dynamically updates the attribute
the browser caches en-US and ignores the change
es only if the change occurs before the page fully loads
explanation: Assistive tech monitors live DOM attributes; updating `lang` dynamically with JavaScript changes the announced language immediately.

question: An HTML file is missing `<!DOCTYPE html>`. The page renders in quirks mode. Which rendering behavior is likely?
options: box model uses content-box instead of border-box
older browsers apply non-standard css interpretation
modern browsers reset doctype assumption and revert to standards mode
the page renders identically to a proper doctype
explanation: Quirks mode activates legacy rendering behaviors to support old websites; modern browsers interpret older CSS rules and may differ from standards mode in box sizing, margins, and padding.

question: A document declares `<html lang='en-US'>` but has no `<head>`. Where do CSS and JavaScript loads go?
options: the browser auto-inserts a head element for them
css and js fail to load because head is required
they are parsed as part of body and loaded in order
the browser rejects the document as malformed
explanation: HTML5 parsers auto-insert missing structural elements (`<head>`, `<body>`) to maintain valid tree structure, so CSS/JS in `<body>` are moved to the inserted `<head>`.

question: Why might `<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width'>` fail on a page served with `<meta http-equiv='X-UA-Compatible' content='IE=5'>`?
options: the x-ua-compatible meta forces internet explorer 5 rendering, ignoring viewport
both metas conflict and only the first one is applied
viewport only works if x-ua-compatible is absent
the x-ua-compatible meta is deprecated and causes parsing errors
explanation: The `X-UA-Compatible` header/meta forces a specific IE rendering mode, which takes precedence; if it targets IE5, modern viewport scaling is disabled.

question: A document has `<meta http-equiv='refresh' content='5; url=http://example.com'>`. Which statement is true?
options: the page redirects after 5 seconds without server involvement
redirect only works if the server sends a matching refresh header
meta refresh is ignored by modern browsers for security
meta refresh only works if placed before meta charset
explanation: The meta refresh directive causes the browser to navigate after the specified delay; it is a client-side redirect that works independently of server headers.

question: A page loads `<link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'>` in head and `<link rel='stylesheet' href='style.css'>` again in body. How many HTTP requests are made?
options: two requests, one for each link tag
one request with caching preventing the second
one request because the browser deduplicates identical links
varies by browser implementation
explanation: Modern browsers cache fetched resources by URL; if the browser fetches the CSS on the first link, the second link request is served from the browser cache without a network round-trip.

question: A document has `<noscript>JavaScript is disabled</noscript>` in the head. When does this appear?
options: only if javascript is disabled at the browser setting level
only if a script tag fails to load or errors
if javascript is not supported or explicitly disabled
noscript only works in body, not in head
explanation: The `<noscript>` element displays its content when the browser does not support JavaScript or when JavaScript is disabled; placement in head is valid and displays before body renders.

question: Why might a page with `<base href='https://example.com/docs/'>` and `<a href='intro.html'>` navigate to an unexpected URL?
options: relative hrefs are resolved against the base, resulting in https://example.com/docs/intro.html
the base element applies only to forms, not anchor links
anchor href ignores base and always uses the current page path
the browser invalidates the href due to base conflicting with the domain
explanation: The `<base>` element sets the base URL for resolving all relative URLs in the document, so `intro.html` becomes `https://example.com/docs/intro.html`.

question: A document has `<head><script src='app.js'></script></head><body>...</body>`. The page is blank until the script finishes loading. Why?
options: script tags in head block html parsing until the script runs
the script must run before the dom is available
browser waits for head to complete before rendering body
an error in the script is preventing body from rendering
explanation: By default, `<script>` tags are render-blocking; the HTML parser pauses while the script loads and executes, delaying initial render until the script completes.
